newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil debt scam probe seen helping fiscal fight.
newsitem.headline: Brazil debt scam probe seen helping fiscal fight.

text.p: Brazil's ongoing probe into a multi-million dollar municipal bond scam may be putting the markets on edge, but economists and political analysts said Monday the inquiry bodes well for the country's fiscal future.

Analysts and economists said the focus on the spending and debt-issuing habits of some states and cities would inevitably lead to further federal controls, boosting Brazil's fight to slash its gaping fiscal deficit.
"This probe is not only of great moral importance, but also of great fiscal importance," said political scientist Murillo Aragao of consultants Arkoadvice.
"The result will be an end to the one loophole states have been able to use to raise money in the market."
The scandal centers on claims that officials and brokers made millions through suspect municipal bond issues.

Senators heading a Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry (CPI) say several states and cities, including financial powerhouse Sao Paulo, issued debt at well below market price to friendly brokerages involved in the scheme.
The instant profits have reportedly made their way to bank accounts in neighbouring Paraguay or possibly the Caribbean.
In addition, states are accused of using the funds raised to cover day-to-day operational costs, when the Constitution stipulates the money can only be used to pay court settlements.
The snowballing allegations are sending a shiver through the markets as the CPI shifts its focus from minor officials to the "big fish" the senators claim are behind the scam.
"There is fear, mainly because people know that an investigation of this nature could get out of control," said economist Mauro Schneider of ING Barings in Sao Paulo.
But Schneider pointed out the probe was likely to "clean up" the states' debt-issuing practices and also the Central Bank's not-entirely watertight auditing procedures.
"A lot of dirt is being pulled out from the carpet. This will have a good effect on public finances," Schneider said.
Brazil posted a public sector operational deficit, which includes debt servicing costs, of 3.89 percent of gross domestic product last year after nearly 5.0 percent in 1995.

The government's aim is to slash that shortfall to 2.5 percent of GDP this year, a target economists consider essential if the inflation-busting Plano Real economic stabilization plan is to be kept on track.
The greatest fear of market watchers and the government is that limelight-seeking senators may demand a CPI of the entire financial system, paralyzing progress of key fiscal reforms.

The Senate has accomplished little since the legislative year started two weeks ago and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has appealed to it to rapidly rewrite a pension reform bill that was savagely mutilated in the Chamber of Deputies.
Both economists and political analysts said they believed the government would be able to keep a lid on the CPI.

They also said the possible involvement of larger banks and senior officials from some of the big pension funds would upset the market, but would not be considered a "crisis" unless important federal government figures were implicated.
Based on the information discovered by the CPI so far, that was unlikely to happen, they said.
